title: 500 Days of Summer
events_chronological: Day 1: Tom sees Summer for the first time when she is introduced as the boss's new assistant at the greeting-card company.
Day 8: Summer overhears Tom playing the Smiths in the lift and tells him she loves them too.
Day 22: at a company karaoke night Summer sings, and Tom's friend McKenzie drunkenly tells her Tom likes her.
Day 27: Summer kisses Tom in the office copy room.
Day 31: Summer tells Tom she does not believe in love and wants nothing serious.
Day 34: they sleep together, and Tom dances through the street to work the next morning.
Day 87: Tom and Summer play house through IKEA and are perfectly happy.
Day 109: Summer shows Tom her bedroom and tells him things she says she has never told anyone.
Day 118: Tom punches a man in a bar for hitting on Summer, and Summer is furious with him for it.
Day 154: a distance has opened between them, and Summer cries at the end of The Graduate.
Day 259: Summer ends the relationship over pancakes in a diner.
Day 290: Tom falls apart at work, drinks through the day and writes a bitter greeting card that gets him hauled in front of his boss.
Day 322: Tom quits the card company to go back to architecture.
Day 402: at a colleague's wedding Summer catches the bouquet, and she and Tom dance and talk warmly all evening.
Day 405: Tom goes to Summer's party expecting a reconciliation and finds an engagement ring on her finger, with the screen splitting his expectations from what actually happens.
Days 450-476: Tom shuts himself in, then his sister Rachel and his own drawings pull him back towards architecture.
Day 488: Summer, now married, finds Tom on their bench and tells him she simply became certain with someone else.
Day 500: Tom meets another candidate, Autumn, at a job interview and asks her out, and the counter resets to Day 1.
syuzhet_notes: An on-screen day counter labels every scene, and the film uses it to cut constantly between the rise and the collapse of the relationship: told-order bullets 1, 3, 5 and 10 jump forward past their neighbours, and bullets 11 and 13 double back behind them, so a happy scene is repeatedly answered by its own aftermath. Told-order bullet 16 runs expectation and reality side by side in split screen, showing one stretch of time twice at once.
fabula_notes: The counter supplies an exact day number for every scene, so the chronology is stated on screen rather than inferred. The weeks covered by told-order bullet 17 are compressed into a single montage.
